paper.citation: Watkins RA, Sugimoto D, Hunt D, Oldham J, Cacolice PA, Stracciolini A. Association of Social Media Use on Sleep Quality and Performance Among Collegiate Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;00:1-7.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional study surveyed 87 NCAA Division III track and field and swimming athletes at two Massachusetts colleges. Social media use was taken from iPhone screen-time data over 7 days, sleep quality from the PROMIS Sleep Disturbance questionnaire, and performance from public meet results (season best or personal record). Athletes using social media for more than 5 hours per day had worse sleep quality than those using 2 hours or less (P=0.033), and higher daily Facebook time was independently associated with lower odds of a season best or personal record (adjusted OR 0.990, 95% CI 0.981-0.999), while total social media time was not.
paper.tldr: In this small cross-sectional study of Division III track and swim athletes, heavier social media use was linked to poorer sleep quality, and more Facebook time was linked to lower odds of a season-best performance, though these associations cannot show cause.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional survey at two NCAA Division III colleges, collected in winter 2020, covering 7-day social media use from iPhone screen-time data, the PROMIS Sleep Disturbance short form, and lifestyle covariates. Athletes were grouped by tertiles of daily social media time (2 hours or less, more than 2 to 5 hours, more than 5 hours). Sleep quality was compared with ANCOVA controlling for romantic relationship status, and performance (season best or personal record from public meet results) was analysed with binary logistic regression after screening confounders. Team-sport athletes were excluded.
paper.findings: Mean social media use was 4.6 +/- 3.4 hours per day. Active users (more than 5 hours per day) had worse PROMIS sleep quality than less active users (2 hours or less; P=0.033), with no difference for moderate users. Their mean t-score of 52.1 stayed below the none-to-slight disturbance cut-off of 55. In the logistic model, Facebook time was associated with lower adjusted odds of a season best or personal record (aOR 0.990, P=0.049), while total social media time was not (aOR 1.002, P=0.103).
paper.limitations: The cross-sectional design gives no causal or long-term information. The sample is small (87 athletes), mostly female, limited to track and field and swimming, and drawn from two colleges. Only five platforms were measured, sleep duration was not assessed, and the authors could not explain why Facebook but not total social media time was associated with performance. The Facebook P value is borderline (0.049).
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use screen-time data as a starting point for conversations about evening phone use, particularly for athletes with very heavy daily social media use, and can include simple sleep hygiene advice. The authors suggest that college social media guidelines may help, but this study alone does not show that reducing social media use improves sleep or performance.
paper.athleteDev: Heavy social media use (more than 5 hours per day) was associated with worse self-reported sleep quality in these athletes, which is relevant to recovery planning for this group. The performance association was weak and limited to Facebook time, so it should not be used as a performance predictor.
paper.rtp: This study does not inform return to sport. It sampled currently rostered athletes, injury status was used only as a covariate, and no return-to-play outcomes were measured, so it cannot guide return timing or clearance.
